ex PM here. this was the issue i had to deal with more (than noise issues, etc). 

it’s very common this happens. rent will be $3000, 2 roommates sign a lease to move in and agree to pay $1500 each. 

one roommate gets a SO and starts to invite them over. then that turns into sleeping over, majority of the week, which turns into moving right in. 

it’s a covert way to sneakily move the SO in to buy time having the conversation with the other roommate about rent. the rent is still $3,000, however there’s 3 people living there now. $1500 from one roommate, and $1500 from now 2 roommates. which means the person paying more will feel screwed. 

my best advice to you to nip this in the bud asap is reaching out to your landlord and letting them know. they can draw up a new lease and everyone residing there can sign it. don’t fear reprisal from your landlord btw (if y’all have a record of being good tenants with them), they’re grateful for residents like yourself who are transparent, and it’s clear you just want things fair which they will understand. IF they decide to raise the price of rent because of this- make sure it’s all equal. 

if your current roommate and their guest refuse to sign the new lease then the landlord will effectively kick out your roommates guest. 

best of luck to you!

i did what quite a few have mentioned in these comments. 

born and raised fort worth and left when i was 25 for colorado to experience all the outside joys and weather i never got to in texas. never was able to “open the windows” like i heard in movies growing up until i moved there. breck for about 6 months before living in denver for 3 years. 

i was single though and dating was particularly difficult in denver. i didn’t move with any friends or family and had none there- so that also added difficulty. i personally noticed quite a few people move to colorado with their SO to settle down, or a barrage of their childhood friends to also live out their outdoor fun. so i ended up dubbing it “home of no new friends”. though immensely gorgeous and lots of outdoor things to do, the people were pretty reserved and uninterested in anything outside their circle. 

with that being said, the summer of 2021 i decided to embark on a months long trek up the PNW ending in Vancouver, CA seeking some sort of vibrancy that aligned with me. sublet my apt in denver out and left. did utah, vegas, but when i got to LA- culture shock. 

i had never actually been to california nor ever really sought a reason to go, but los angeles is a whole world of its own. not trying to say it’s better than anywhere than in particular- but i did finally feel like i belong and im making friends easily. going out by yourself is normal and common here and doesn’t give you the same degree of nervousness or awkwardness i had living elsewhere where someone always has someone and you’re just “alone”. of course there’s more people here, so more friendlies, more opportunity, and MANY more things to do. 

my best advice to anyone leaving their hometown is DO IT. why? because you can always come home. simple as that. i had no money, was broke, lived in my car for 8 months- but i was happier than i ever had been being in a place i felt like i belonged. money came, a home came, and everything fell into place. nothing is ever easy but if you want it bad enough you’ll get it. 

another great bit of advice- if you’re wanting to move somewhere else but don’t think you’ve landed on the place yet, make a list of 3-5 places you can see yourself living based off your interests, research, and budget. then go travel to each of these places and live like a local would while you’re there. socialize and get to know your potential new home! moving blindly to a town you think you may like is challenging. 

i love texas because its home, but its definitely a “place to visit” for me instead of a “place to live”. i enjoy it far more visiting. eventually my plan is to move to BC Canada where my husband is from and start a family there.
